data.title: Stewardship and Khalifah
data.sourcePassage: Christianity teaches that God created the world and declared it 'very good' (Genesis 1:31). Humans are not the owners of the earth but its stewards — responsible managers on God's behalf. The earth belongs to God: 'The earth belongs to God, and everything in it' (Psalm 24:1). This means humans have a duty to care for creation, not exploit it. The growing Eco-Church movement in Britain shows Christian communities putting stewardship into practice through solar panels, reduced waste, and sustainable purchasing. Islam teaches a similar concept: khalifah, meaning steward or trustee. Humans are entrusted with Allah's creation and accountable to God for how they treat it. The Qur'an emphasises mizan — the balance of creation — and condemns israf (waste and excess). 'Do not commit excess. Indeed, Allah does not like those who commit excess' (Qur'an 7:31). Muslim environmental organisations like IFEES work to connect Islamic teaching to practical environmental action. Both traditions see environmental care not as an optional preference but as a religious obligation.

data.title: Ahimsa, Interdependence, and Sewa
data.sourcePassage: Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism each offer distinctive foundations for environmental responsibility. Hinduism teaches that Brahman — ultimate reality — is present in all of creation: in animals, rivers, trees, and the earth. This makes the natural world inherently sacred. The principle of ahimsa (non-violence) extends to all living beings, motivating vegetarianism and care for animals and the environment. The Ganges and other rivers are considered sacred in Hinduism, making their pollution not only an environmental crisis but a religious one. Buddhism teaches interdependence (pratityasamutpada): all things arise in connection with each other, and nothing exists in isolation. This means that harming the environment harms the whole web of life — including ourselves. Right Livelihood in the Eightfold Path includes not earning a living through environmentally destructive work. Mindful consumption encourages Buddhists to buy and use only what is truly needed, not what craving demands. Sikhism teaches that Waheguru created everything and is present in all creation. Caring for creation is an act of sewa (selfless service) and a form of devotion. EcoSikh is a Sikh environmental organisation working globally on tree planting and clean water projects.

data.title: Environmental Justice and Human Responsibility
data.sourcePassage: Environmental justice is the principle that environmental benefits and harms should be fairly distributed. In reality, this is often not the case. The countries that have contributed least to global carbon emissions — often the poorest nations — tend to suffer the most severe consequences of climate change: floods, droughts, and food shortages. Within wealthy countries, poorer communities are often located near polluting industries and face higher levels of environmental harm. Religious and non-religious traditions connect this to wider concerns about justice. Islamic teaching on adl (justice) demands that environmental damage is not simply displaced onto the poor. Christian charities like CAFOD and Tearfund explicitly connect climate justice to their global poverty work. Humanists argue that reason and concern for human wellbeing require acting on evidence about environmental damage, and that wealthier nations bear greater responsibility because they have caused more harm. Both individual action and government or collective action are important: individual choices send market signals and express values, but the scale of climate change requires international agreements and structural change. Religious communities can shape both.
